blocks.content: An object's life has four stages. Everything else in this topic is a detail of one of these four.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/b18093ad-5f9f-43a5-8110-9a184b7742bb.png

ANALOGY: A HOTEL GUEST

A guest checks in (creation) → uses the room (in use) → checks out (unreachable  no more key) → hotel cleans and reassigns the room (garbage collection). 

The room (memory) is available for the next guest only after housekeeping is done.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 1. Phase 1: Creation
An object's life starts the moment you write new. Under the hood, three things happen in order:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/fae6d6fc-1fa7-4438-b7e7-20ca40ded73f.png

["Memory is allocated: The JVM creates space for the new object in the heap.
","Default initialization happens: All instance variables get default values (0,false,null, etc.).
","Constructor executes: The constructor runs and assigns the actual values defined by your program.
"]
items: Memory is allocated: The JVM creates space for the new object in the heap.
Default initialization happens: All instance variables get default values (0,false,null, etc.).
Constructor executes: The constructor runs and assigns the actual values defined by your program.

blocks.content: WHAT MYCAR ACTUALLY HOLDS
myCar is a variable on the stack. It doesn't hold the object it holds a reference (address) to the object sitting on the heap. The object and the variable are two separate things.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/9972bd71-7d90-484d-ae8f-1a93c574e059.png
2. Phase 2: In Use
Once created, an object lives as long as something holds a reference to it. During this phase you call methods, read fields, and change state.

myCar.speed = 200;                 // changing state
String info = myCar.brand;        // reading state
myCar.accelerate();               // calling a method

blocks.content: An object can be referenced by many variables at once. All of them see the same object.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/13e5d2ff-8064-4c5d-9d0d-467a65d08d8c.png
3. Phase 3: Becoming Unreachable

An object becomes unreachable when no variable in the program holds a reference to it anymore. At this point the object is useless but the memory is not yet freed. It is now eligible for garbage collection.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/dcc1f288-ca87-484b-8193-4b46a3311adf.png
Three common ways an object loses all its references:

codes.python:
class Car:
    def __init__(self, brand, speed):
        self.brand = brand
        self.speed = speed


def place_order():
    delivery_car = Car("Ford", 120)
    # delivery_car goes out of scope when the function returns, object becomes unreachable


if __name__ == "__main__":
    place_order()

    car = Car("Honda", 100)
    car = Car("BMW", 200)          # Honda Car is now unreachable

    temp = Car("Kia", 90)
    temp = None                     # Kia Car is now unreachable
    print("done")

blocks.content: 4. Phase 4: Garbage Collection
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/57fc493f-520d-42b1-8b4a-d2a1e4d4c96f.png
Java manages memory automatically through a Garbage Collector (GC). You never call free() like in C. The GC runs in the background, finds objects with no references, and reclaims their memory.

ANALOGY: HOTEL HOUSEKEEPING

Once a guest checks out (no more reference), the room doesn't magically clean itself the moment they leave. 

Housekeeping (the GC) comes around on its own schedule, checks which rooms are empty, and cleans them for the next guest. 

You don't control when you just guarantee the room will eventually be cleaned.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: Key things to understand about GC:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/4e878b08-a1d2-4b2d-8589-7878a6a97db4.png
You cansuggest GC withSystem.gc()but the JVM is free to ignore it. Don't rely on it. Design your code so objects become unreachable naturally the GC handles the rest.
5. Stack vs Heap
This trips up a lot of beginners. The short version:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/e8dea6d6-b236-4df8-b856-affd94116d48.png
ANALOGY: WHITEBOARD VS WAREHOUSE

The stack is a whiteboard you write on it while working, erase it when done, fast and temporary. The heap is a warehouse objects are stored there for as long as needed, removed only when nobody wants them anymore.
6. finalize(): The Old Cleanup Hook
Java used to provide a method called finalize() that the GC would call just before destroying an object. The idea: you could do last-minute cleanup there (close a file, release a resource).
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512784783-321470876.png
blocks.alt: Timeline showing finalize only runs if the GC happens to run before JVM exit, otherwise it never executes

blocks.content: finalize() is deprecated since Java 9and removed in Java 18. It's unpredictable (you don't know when it runs), slow (delays GC), and dangerous (can accidentally resurrect objects). Never use it in new code.
What to use instead
Use try-with-resources for anything that needs cleanup (files, connections, streams). It's guaranteed, immediate, and clean.

codes.python:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    with open("data.txt", "w") as f:
        f.write("hello")

    with open("data.txt", "r") as reader:
        print(reader.read())
    # reader.close() called automatically here, even if an exception occurs

blocks.content: 7. Manual vs Automatic Memory Management

Java and Python are garbage collected languages, the runtime decides when memory is reclaimed. Languages like C and C++ are manually managed, the programmer is responsible for freeing every byte that was allocated. Both approaches solve the same problem, deciding when an object’s memory can be reused, but they place the responsibility in different hands.
Garbage collected languages: Java and Python
blocks.text: Garbage collected languages: Java and Python

blocks.content: Java’s JVM uses a tracing garbage collector. Periodically it walks the object graph starting from root references, local variables, static fields, active threads, and marks everything reachable. Anything left unmarked is garbage and its memory is reclaimed. Python’s CPython interpreter uses a different primary mechanism, reference counting. Every object carries a count of how many references point to it, and when that count hits zero the object is freed immediately. Because reference counting alone cannot detect reference cycles, two objects that only reference each other, CPython also runs a periodic cyclic garbage collector to catch those cases.
Manually managed languages: C and C++
blocks.text: Manually managed languages: C and C++

blocks.content: In C, the programmer calls malloc to request memory and free to release it. In C++, new and delete play the same role, and modern C++ leans heavily on RAII, Resource Acquisition Is Initialization, where an object’s destructor automatically releases its resources the moment the object goes out of scope. There is no runtime deciding when memory is reclaimed, the programmer’s code is the only thing that decides.

codes.python:
class Car:
    def __init__(self, brand, speed):
        self.brand = brand
        self.speed = speed

    def accelerate(self):
        self.speed += 10


if __name__ == "__main__":
    car = Car("BMW", 200)   # reference counting keeps the object alive
    car.accelerate()
    del car                  # removes this reference, not a manual free

    # there is no dangling pointer here, 'car' is simply unbound now.
    # the next line is commented out because it would raise NameError,
    # not undefined behavior, this is shown for illustration only
    # car.accelerate()        # NameError: name 'car' is not defined

    print("reference removed; the commented line would raise NameError, not corrupt memory")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content:
ANALOGY: VALET VS SELF PARK

Garbage collection is valet parking, you hand over the car (object) and staff decide when to bring it back around for the next customer. You never touch the keys again.

Manual memory management is self park, you personally have to walk back and move your own car out. Forget, and the spot stays blocked forever, that is a leak. Move a car that has already been given to someone else, and you crash into things that are not yours anymore, that is a dangling pointer.
8. Common Lifecycle Bugs
Garbage collection removes an entire category of bugs, but lifecycle bugs still show up in every language. They just take a different shape.
Dangling references and use after close
blocks.text: Dangling references and use after close

blocks.content: In C and C++, using a pointer after its memory has been freed is called use after free, and it is undefined behavior, the program might crash, or worse, silently corrupt data. Java and Python cannot have that exact bug, because an object cannot be collected while a live reference to it still exists. But an equivalent mistake shows up whenever a resource is used after it has been explicitly closed, for example reading from a file handle or a database connection after calling close on it.
Memory leaks in garbage collected languages
blocks.text: Memory leaks in garbage collected languages

blocks.content: A garbage collector only frees objects that are unreachable. It has no idea whether a reachable object is still logically useful. A memory leak in Java or Python happens when something keeps a reference to an object that the program will never actually use again, so the collector correctly, but unhelpfully, keeps it alive forever.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512786778-312367557.png
blocks.alt: A screen stays registered on an event bus after navigating away, so the bus still references it and the garbage collector can never reclaim it

blocks.content: ["Static fields or static collections that keep accumulating objects and are never cleared","Listeners or callbacks registered on a long lived object, such as an event bus or a singleton, and never unregistered","Caches with no eviction policy or size limit, so every entry ever added stays in memory","Non-static inner classes in Java, which silently hold a reference to their enclosing instance","ThreadLocal values that are set on a pooled thread but never removed, so they outlive the task that created them"]
items: Static fields or static collections that keep accumulating objects and are never cleared
Listeners or callbacks registered on a long lived object, such as an event bus or a singleton, and never unregistered
Caches with no eviction policy or size limit, so every entry ever added stays in memory
Non-static inner classes in Java, which silently hold a reference to their enclosing instance
ThreadLocal values that are set on a pooled thread but never removed, so they outlive the task that created them

blocks.title: A leak that looks harmless
blocks.text: A screen registers itself as a listener on a global event bus when it opens, but never unregisters when the user navigates away. The screen object is still referenced by the event bus, so it stays in memory. Do this across a long running application and old screens pile up until the app runs out of memory, even though every individual screen was, technically, garbage collectible.

blocks.content: 9. Deterministic Cleanup: try-with-resources and Context Managers
blocks.text: 9. Deterministic Cleanup: try-with-resources and Context Managers

blocks.content: Garbage collection guarantees that memory is eventually reclaimed, but it makes no promises about when. That is fine for memory, but it is not fine for things like open files, network sockets, and database connections, which need to be released the moment you are done with them, not whenever the collector happens to run.
Java: AutoCloseable and try-with-resources

Any class that implements the AutoCloseable interface can be used in a try-with-resources block. The JVM guarantees that close is called at the end of the block, even if an exception is thrown inside it.
Python: context managers in more depth
blocks.text: Python: context managers in more depth

blocks.content: The with statement calls __enter__ when entering the block and __exit__ when leaving it, whether the block finished normally or raised an exception. This is why Python code almost always opens files with with open(path) as f, instead of calling open and close by hand.

codes.python:
from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def managed_file(path):
    f = open(path, "r")
    try:
        yield f
    finally:
        f.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with open("data.txt", "w") as f:
        f.write("hello from managed file")

    with managed_file("data.txt") as f:
        print(f.read())
    # f.close() runs even if the block raises an exception

blocks.content: Why finalizers and destructors are not the answer
blocks.text: Why finalizers and destructors are not the answer

blocks.content: Java’s old finalize method and Python’s __del__ both run only when the garbage collector decides to collect the object, and that timing is not guaranteed. An exception raised inside one of these methods can be silently swallowed. In CPython, an object caught in a reference cycle may not have __del__ called promptly, or at all, until the cyclic collector runs. Deterministic constructs, try-with-resources, the with statement, and RAII destructors in C++, tie cleanup to a scope in your code, not to memory pressure, so they run exactly when you expect.
If cleanup has to happen at a specific moment, it does not belong in a finalizer or a destructor callback triggered by the collector, it belongs in an explicit close tied to a scope.

items: Every object goes through 4 stages: Creation → In Use → Unreachable → Garbage Collected.
Creation happens in 3 steps: heap memory allocated → default values set → constructor runs.
The variable holds a reference (address), not the object itself. The object lives on the heap.
Multiple variables can point to the same object changing the object through one variable is visible through all others.
An object becomes unreachable when all references to it are gone (out of scope, reassigned, or set to null).
Garbage Collection is automatic and non-deterministic you can't predict exactly when it runs.
Stack = fast, temporary, per-method. Heap = larger, managed by GC, object lifetime.
finalize() is deprecated. Use try-with-resources for resource cleanup.
Garbage collected languages like Java and Python let the runtime decide when memory is freed. Manually managed languages like C and C++ make the programmer call free or delete explicitly.

A memory leak in a garbage collected language happens when something keeps referencing an object the program no longer needs, common causes are static collections, unregistered listeners, and caches with no eviction.
Using a resource after it has been closed, such as reading from a closed file or connection, is the garbage collected world’s version of use after free.
try-with-resources in Java and the with statement in Python give deterministic cleanup, tied to a scope, not to whenever the collector happens to run.
